Nookimisuk, les grands-mères accueillent: Nookimisuk, the grandmothers, welcome women home.
La chaleur de la main d’une mère est for: The warmth of a mother’s hand is strong and loving. The memory of it nourishes us, or leaves its mark if something was missing. That is where a grandmother can step in. Indigenous grandmothers disrupt existing colonial systems with their community wisdom. They are asking Canada to close the gap between what governments and decision-makers say and what they do. “We want our grandmothers to regain their rightful place in our communities,” says Isabelle Meawasige, herself a grandmother. She belongs to the Bear Clan of Serpent River, and her roots are Ojibwe and Algonquin.
Dans une<l1> lettre adressée aux Nations: In a letter to the United Nations on the occasion of the 50th session of the Human Rights Council, she points out that the research and voices of Indigenous women are not at the heart of efforts to fight violence against Indigenous women and girls in Canada. Meawasige, who is 72, worked as a social worker for more than 30 years. She describes the link between extractive industries and violence against women. Some of her relatives are missing. Her home territory is suffering the damage caused by the mining and forestry industries’ Man Camps (temporary work camps). Meawasige is the lead grandmother of Kii-Ga-Do-Waak Nookimisuk, the grandmothers’ council that fights sexual violence, exploitation and human trafficking in Indigenous communities in Ontario by nurturing and restoring traditional responsibilities and roles. “The existing political, economic and social structures in Canada appear unable to transform attitudes and implement policies that would effectively end violence against Indigenous women,” they say in their letter, which supports the report of the UN Special Rapporteur. According to the findings of the Polaris Project, the number of reported human trafficking crisis cases has risen by 40% since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. The scale of the phenomenon is enormous: according to the International Labour Organization, it affected nearly 25 million people worldwide in January 2021.
<strong>Lien entre l’exploitation du ter: The link between exploitation of the land and violence against women
Comme l’indique le site web de Kii-Ga-Do: As the Kii-Ga-Do-Waak website explains, the grandmothers’ council sees a connection between colonialism and the dispossession of land, as well as a correlation with violence against women. United Nations reports have found that human trafficking increases in regions where the natural environment is under threat, and that there are links between gender-based violence and environmental crimes. Jacqueline St-Pierre works at Kii-Ga-Do-Waak. She takes on several roles, including communications, fundraising and coordination, in addition to being an adopted granddaughter.
« Les industries extractives du colonial: “The extractive industries of colonialism couldn’t do what they do if people stayed connected to the land,” she says. The organization<l1> Indigenous Climate Action (ICA)</l1> describes how the extraction and exploitation of resources and fossil fuels on the land perpetuate violence against women. “The resources taken from our lands contaminate the environment and damage ecosystems, while increasing greenhouse gases (GHGs) in the atmosphere, which worsens climate change,” reads one report. It explains that<l2> these activities</l2> give rise to temporary work camps, resulting in an increase in sex trafficking and violence against women, says the ICA. The UN Special Rapporteur, James Anaya, made this finding in 2014. “Indigenous women have reported that the influx of workers into Indigenous communities has also led to an increase in cases of sexual harassment and violence, including rape and assault,” he stated. “Women were the ones who maintained the connection to the land,” says Ms. St-Pierre. That connection was reinforced by the teaching and practice of traditional medicine. The separation of mothers and children, notably because children were sent to residential schools, severed the connection to the land. Meawasige notes that the last residential school closed in 1996, that survivors are still alive and are still raising their children today. They were sent back home and had to cope with the hardships and trauma they had endured. Economic instability and social disruption make people more vulnerable to the dangerous tactics used to exploit them. The National Inquiry into Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls, whose report is titled “Reclaiming Power and Place,” was a public inquiry held in response to Call to Action 41 of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada. The inquiry found that, “despite their different circumstances and backgrounds, all missing and murdered persons are linked by economic, social and political marginalization, racism and misogyny woven into the fabric of Canadian society.” The mandate of the national inquiry was to examine existing institutional policies and practices that address or perpetuate violence. The letter to the UN points to a flaw: the final report implicitly establishes that “violence is the intersection of ongoing colonialism with domestic violence that has infiltrated Indigenous homes and communities.”
« Une des considérations essentielles po: “One of the essential considerations for maintaining good relationships is to challenge the false but prevailing perception that Indigenous peoples are at the heart of the problem,” reads the letter Kii-Ga-Do-Waak sent to the UN.
Kii-Ga-Do-Waak Nookimisukl se consacre à: Kii-Ga-Do-Waak Nookimisuk is dedicated to healing through traditional ceremonies and teachings and rites of passage. Through gatherings, education and training, the grandmothers help people understand the nature of the sexual violence and exploitation committed against Indigenous peoples. The grandmothers work with women and girls who have been victims of human trafficking.
« On les amène dans une tente, et elles: “We take them to a tent, and they spend two or three days there fasting. They share, they build bonds. And when they’re ready, they go to a sweat lodge, where they return to the womb of the earth. They can be reborn in that lodge,” explains Meawasige. The grandmothers sing for them as they come out of the sweat lodge. “Very, very powerful things happen.” A fire keeper tends the sacred fire. The participants can offer their prayers and offerings to this sacred fire. It is there that they can shed everything they no longer need to carry.
« Là, elles peuvent tout laisser aller,: “There, they can let everything go, they can release all the wounds,” says Meawasige. When they come out, the grandmothers are there, arms outstretched with towels to wrap around them. Meawasige tells the story of a young woman who was a victim of human trafficking. “She disappeared from her community without anyone making a fuss. Nobody said goodbye to her,” she says. When this woman was able to get out of her situation, the grandmothers decided to hold a circle in her honour, which they named Welcome Home. Meawasige went to speak to the chief of the young woman’s nation and told him her story. He came to the grandmothers’ circle and welcomed her home. When she came out of the sweat lodge, “the grandmothers wrapped her in a blanket, and the young woman fell to the ground, her heart on the ground,” Meawasige continues. The grandmothers have a teaching that says that if a woman’s heart is on the ground, there is no hope. “No matter how strong these warriors are, no matter how many bullets or which way the arrow is pointing, if the woman’s heart is on the ground, you might as well give up,” the grandmother explains. The grandmothers lifted her off the ground. And they rocked her. The whole time, they sang her a song that said: “I will always love you.”
« Voilà une autre femme qui est rentrée: “There’s another woman who has come home. She was home; her body, her mind and her soul were home too,” shares Meawasige. “It’s as if they’ve been cleansed and made light. Their whole body shows it, their face glows, they shine from the inside and the outside.” Why can grandmothers take on a role that mothers struggle to fill? “Maybe it’s because it takes a long time to heal from early childhood trauma,” notes Meawasige. And it is because grandmothers have always played this role that this energy is still alive and drives Meawasige and her circle of women to be grandmothers to those who need them most.
<strong>Les grands-mères autochtones ont: Indigenous grandmothers have an essential leadership role
Les grands-mères jouent un rôle particul: Grandmothers play a special role in Anishinaabe customs. Ms. St-Pierre has often heard the grandmothers say “that their own customs were like embers that had to be buried. And right now, they are fanning the flames, to rekindle the fire of matrilineal customs.”
« Dans nos communautés, en tant que gran: “In our communities, as grandmothers, we have a lot of power. We have a lot of voice,” explains Meawasige. “And people are very, very hungry for grandmothers’ knowledge. When the grandmothers’ fires are lit, people travel miles to come to that fire and pray with those grandmothers.” In the letter to the UN, Meawasige explains that the calls for justice “demand greater visibility and greater participation of Indigenous women, not as subjects of research, but as agents of change in decision-making processes on new policies and systemic transformation.”
Les grands-mères autochtones ont « un rô: Indigenous grandmothers have “a vital leadership role in their communities, which they continue to carry out, [but they] are not recognized as holders of their cultural rights within traditional governance systems,” the letter to the UN states. In addition, as the grandmothers’ council explains, Canadian government systems create barriers to accessing sustainable funding for their cultural and political work. Policy changes and occasional funding are not enough, despite the data and reports such as those from the Sisters in Spirit campaign of the Native Women’s Association of Canada (2009), the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (2015) and the National Inquiry into Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls (2019). The letter to the UN points out: “(...) too often, resources are channelled to national Indigenous organizations, without regard for the efforts of grassroots Indigenous women. A consistent and ongoing distribution of funds is needed and must support the efforts of grassroots women, particularly grandmothers.” “It’s a very difficult time right now,” acknowledges Meawasige. “We can’t bring our people together and tell them these stories that will flow in their blood and make them young again.” But the pandemic is not stopping the grandmothers. They continue their work by making phone calls and holding video conferences. Kii-Ga-Do-Waak Nookimisuk is raising funds to make a documentary, with filming set to begin in the spring. The project, called<l1> The Nokomis Project</l1>, will serve as a permanent archive of the grandmothers’ initiatives. A grandmother’s voice has power: the power to teach girls and women and to heal them. That power is a testament to the strength of love.
